title: Representation and Verification of Domain-Based Application Service Identity within Internet PKI Using X.509 Certificates
summary: Specifies procedures for representing and verifying the identity of application services using X.509 certificates in the context of TLS, such as checking that a certificate really matches the server name the client meant to reach. It is a proposed standard and was replaced by RFC 9525.

plainLanguage.summary: When a program connects to a service over TLS, it checks the certificate the service sends back against the name it was looking for. This RFC gives one shared set of rules for that check, so that a web browser, a mail program and a phone all agree on what a certificate has to contain. It also says where the name should live in the certificate, and rules out the wildcard certificates that let one certificate cover a whole domain.

questions: how to verify server identity in tls certificate
what is a dns-id in a certificate
when to use the common name for hostname checks
subtitle: How a client decides that the certificate it was given really names the service it asked for.

tldr.problem: Every application protocol that used TLS had its own rules for naming a server in a certificate and for checking that the certificate matched the name the client wanted. The differences confused certificate authorities, application developers and protocol designers.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines four identifier types, a CN-ID, a DNS-ID, an SRV-ID and a URI-ID, and a matching procedure. The client builds a list of reference identifiers from the name it expected, then checks them against the identifiers the server presented in its certificate, label by label and case-insensitively.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6125 is a Proposed Standard from March 2011 and has been obsoleted by RFC 9525, which restates the same rules for checking that a TLS certificate names the service the client asked for.

facts.label: Reference list rule
facts.value: Must be built independently of the server's certificate

facts.label: Common Name fallback
facts.value: Only when no DNS-ID, SRV-ID or URI-ID is present

facts.label: Label comparison
facts.value: Case-insensitive ASCII, every label must match

today: RFC 6125 is a Proposed Standard from March 2011, and it has been obsoleted by RFC 9525, which restates the same rules for representing and verifying domain-based application service identity in TLS certificates. The RFC notes that it does not supersede the certificate issuance and validation rules of RFC 5280, which remain authoritative.

sections.title: Why Service Identity Needed Common Rules
sections.content:
Almost everything on the Internet is a client talking to a server over TLS. The client has an idea of who it is talking to, such as the website at example.com, and the server answers with a public key certificate issued by a certification authority. The client has to check that the identity the certificate carries matches the identity the client expected.

Each application protocol used to invent its own rules for that check, and the differences confused certification authorities, application developers and protocol designers. This RFC gives one set of recommended procedures for representing and verifying service identity in certificates used with TLS.

The direction of travel is clear. Certification authorities should stop putting domain names in the Common Name field and start putting them in the subjectAltName extension, as a dNSName entry, and to use more specific identifier types where the protocol calls for them. Issuers should stop handing out wildcard certificates. The document applies only to fully qualified DNS domain names, only to TLS and DTLS, and only to PKIX systems. Client identities, IP address certificates, other security protocols and certification authority policy are all out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: Every secure connection starts with a certificate, and the client has to decide whether the certificate names the service it meant to reach. Different programs used to answer that question differently. This RFC gives them one set of answers to follow.

sections.title: Presented Identifiers and Reference Identifiers
sections.content:
The RFC splits the naming question in two. The reference identifier is what the client expects: an identifier built from the source domain the client was given and, optionally, the type of service it is connecting to. The presented identifier is what the server puts in its certificate. The check is whether one presented identifier matches one reference identifier.

Four identifier types matter. A CN-ID is a Common Name in the certificate's subject field whose value has the shape of a domain name. A DNS-ID is a subjectAltName entry of type dNSName. An SRV-ID is a subjectAltName entry of the otherName form called SRVName, which carries a service name such as _imaps.example.net. A URI-ID is a subjectAltName entry of type uniformResourceIdentifier whose value holds both a scheme and a host part, such as sip:voice.example.edu.

The types differ along two lines. A CN-ID and a DNS-ID are direct, meaning a person or a configuration supplies them, and unrestricted, meaning the same certificate can be used for any service type. An SRV-ID is restricted to one service type and may be either direct or derived. A URI-ID is direct and restricted. The RFC also defines the source domain, the fully qualified domain name the client expects, and the derived domain, one the client worked out for itself, for example through a DNS SRV lookup.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC uses two terms. The reference identifier is the name the client expects. The presented identifier is the name the server's certificate carries. Four kinds of name can play either part: a Common Name in the subject field, a dNSName entry, an SRV service name and a URI with a host part.

sections.title: How a Certificate Should Name a Server
sections.content:
These are the rules for the certification authority that issues the certificate. The certificate should include a DNS-ID if at all possible, because that is the baseline for interoperability. If the protocol the certificate secures calls for an SRV-ID or a URI-ID, the certificate should include one; for a URI-ID the scheme must be the one for that protocol and the host part must be the fully qualified domain name of the service.

Even though many deployed clients still look at the Common Name, authorities are encouraged to stop issuing certificates that put the domain name there, and the certificate should not include a CN-ID unless a specification that reuses this one asks for it. A certificate may hold more than one DNS-ID, SRV-ID or URI-ID, but should not hold more than one CN-ID. Unless a reusing specification allows wildcards, the domain name part of an identifier should not contain the wildcard character, either as a whole left-most label such as *.example.com or as a fragment such as f*o.example.com.

The service provider's side has a matching rule. If a certificate might be used for any type of service, request one with only a DNS-ID. If it will serve a single type of service, request a DNS-ID plus an SRV-ID or URI-ID that limits it to that service type. A provider offering several service types who wants to limit each certificate is encouraged to ask for one certificate per service type rather than one certificate carrying many SRV-IDs or URI-IDs.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules for the certificate authority are simple. Put the domain name in the subjectAltName extension as a dNSName, add an SRV or URI name only when the protocol asks for one, and leave the Common Name out. The service provider asks for the identifiers it actually needs: one plain dNSName for a general-purpose certificate, or a name that also pins down the service type.

sections.title: How a Client Verifies the Server's Identity
sections.content:
The client builds a list of acceptable reference identifiers from the source domain and, where the protocol uses them, the service type. It must build that list independently of the identifiers the server presents, so that a certificate cannot steer the check. The list should include a DNS-ID, and should include an SRV-ID if servers for that service are usually found through DNS SRV records, and a URI-ID if the protocol associates a URI with the service. A CN-ID may be included for compatibility with deployed infrastructure.

The server's identifiers arrive in its certificate. The client checks each reference identifier against the presented identifiers until one matches, and stops there. Before comparing, it splits each identifier into a domain name part and a service type part: for an SRV-ID such as _imaps.example.net the domain is example.net and the service type is imaps; for a URI-ID such as sip:voice.example.edu the domain is voice.example.edu and the service type is sip.

The comparison rules are exact. For a traditional domain name the labels are compared with a case-insensitive ASCII comparison, and every label must match. For an internationalized domain name, any U-label is converted to an A-label first and then compared the same way. When a presented identifier contains a wildcard, the client should not treat a wildcard in any label other than the left-most one as a match, and if the wildcard is the whole left-most label it should compare only against the left-most label of the reference identifier, so *.example.com matches foo.example.com but not bar.foo.example.com or example.com.

A Common Name is checked only as a last resort: if and only if the certificate has no DNS-ID, SRV-ID, URI-ID or other application-specific identifier that the client supports. There are two outcomes when nothing matches. If the user has already pinned this certificate to one of the reference identifiers, the check succeeds when the presented certificate matches the pinned one. Otherwise an interactive client should tell the user about the mismatch and end the attempt with a bad certificate error, and an automated client should end the attempt the same way and log the error.
sections.plainLanguage: The client works out what names it will accept before it looks at the certificate, so the server cannot influence the check. It then compares each accepted name with the names in the certificate, one label at a time and without regard to case. If nothing matches, the connection fails, unless the user has already pinned that certificate to the name in the past.

sections.title: Wildcards, Pinning and Confusable Names
sections.content:
The security section explains why the rules are stricter than those of the older application protocols summarized in Appendix B. A wildcard certificate vouches for every host name in its domain at once, which is convenient for administrators and a risk for rogue or badly configured hosts. The older specifications are also unclear about where the wildcard character may sit: only as the whole left-most label, as a fragment of it, in another label, on a public suffix such as co.uk, more than once in a label, or in more than one label. That ambiguity lets different clients behave differently and pushes complexity into the checking code.

There is no specification for embedding the wildcard character inside the A-label or U-label of an internationalized domain name, so implementations are strongly discouraged from including it or checking for it there. A presented identifier may still carry the wildcard as the whole left-most label while the remaining labels are ordinary ones.

Pinning is the escape hatch for a name mismatch: the user explicitly accepts a certificate that names a different domain, and the client remembers that association. The RFC says the remembered association must take account of both the certificate and the context in which it was accepted, including the chain up to the trust anchor, the source domain, the service type, the derived domain and the port. Allowing internationalized names in certificates also opens the door to visually similar characters, so the document points at the confusable character work for that. Finally, the RFC allows several DNS-IDs, SRV-IDs or URI-IDs in one certificate because the TLS Server Name Indication extension lets the client ask for the name it wants, but it discourages several CN-IDs.
sections.plainLanguage: Wildcards are the main worry. A certificate with a wildcard covers every host under a domain at once, and the older rules disagree about where the wildcard may go, so two clients can disagree about what a certificate covers. Pinning is the deliberate way for a user to accept a certificate that names a different domain, and the client has to remember the circumstances of that decision, not just the certificate.

sections.title: A Checklist for Protocol Designers
sections.content:
The RFC ends with a short checklist for anyone writing an application protocol. If the technology uses DNS SRV records to find application services, consider requiring support for the SRV-ID identifier type. If it uses URIs to identify services, consider requiring the URI-ID type. If it needs domain names in the Common Name for backward compatibility, consider supporting CN-ID as a fallback. If it needs the wildcard character, consider supporting wildcard certificates and say exactly where the wildcard may appear, for example only as the complete left-most label.

The point of the checklist is that a protocol specification should state which identifier types servers and clients must support, which ones issuers should include and which ones a service provider should ask for, because those answers differ from one application to the next. Appendix A gives sample text that a protocol can reuse.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC gives protocol designers a short list of questions to answer when they write their own rules: should clients accept a service name, a URI, a Common Name or a wildcard? Each protocol should say which of those it requires, because the answer is different for web, mail and voice services.

viz.caption: THE VERIFICATION PROCEDURE, SUMMARISED FROM RFC 6125 SECTION 6.1

data.title: Verifying service identity
data.code:
1. Build a list of acceptable reference identifiers from the
   source domain and, optionally, the application service type.
2. Take the server's presented identifiers from its PKIX certificate.
3. Check each reference identifier against the presented identifiers.
4. When comparing, match the source domain and, optionally, the
   application service type.
